analysis.one_liner: Loosens US trade-injury rules so tariffs and quotas are easier to win against imports.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by six Democrats and one Republican, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite US trade remedy laws to make it much easier for domestic industries to win protection from imports. It lowers the legal bar for showing that imports hurt a US industry, tells the International Trade Commission to weigh evidence in ways that favor petitioners, adds special rules for seasonal farm products, and creates a new Commerce Department permit-and-monitoring program for every steel shipment entering the country. The practical effect would be more tariffs and quotas on imported goods — especially steel — which raise prices for US manufacturers that buy those goods and for consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: US producers in import-sensitive industries, above all steelmakers, gain the most: easier injury tests mean faster and more frequent tariffs and quotas on competitors' products, and the steel import certificate program gives the industry weekly, shipment-level visibility into competitors' volumes and sources. Seasonal fruit and vegetable growers also gain from rules allowing them to claim injury on a season-by-season basis. Workers in those industries benefit indirectly to the extent protection preserves jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the requirement that imports be a 'substantial cause' of serious industry injury with a much lower bar — imports need only 'contribute significantly' to injury, even if other causes were larger — making safeguard tariffs far easier to obtain [S2][S3].

Tells the International Trade Commission to judge antidumping and countervailing duty cases using factors that favor petitioners: ignoring import volume when assessing price effects, focusing only on the 'merchant market' when producers sell internally, and not weighing other causes of injury against the import contribution [S2][S3].

Creates a steel import notification certificate program: every steel shipment needs a Commerce Department permit before entry, with weekly public release of shipment-level data — a monitoring tool the domestic steel industry can use to build future trade cases [S2][S3].
Lets unions, firms, or worker groups ask the President to have the ITC monitor imports of any product for up to two years when injury is alleged, lowering the cost of starting a trade case [S2][S3].

Allows producers of perishable agricultural products to be treated as a separate industry each season and to count unpicked crops and abandoned acreage as evidence of injury, making seasonal dumping cases easier to win [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Downstream US industries that buy steel and other protected goods — construction, autos, appliances, machinery — would pay more for inputs, and consumers would pay more for finished goods, since tariffs and quotas raise domestic prices. Importers, retailers, and foreign exporters would face new permit paperwork, fees, and restricted market access. Trade partners, including Canada and Mexico, would face the same remedies on their goods.

drawbacks.text: Tariffs and quotas raise prices for the industries that use the protected goods as inputs; US steel users have historically employed far more workers than steelmakers, so protection can cost more jobs downstream than it saves upstream (general knowledge about how tariffs work).

Telling the commission not to weigh import volume against price effects, and to disregard other causes of injury, removes balance from a quasi-judicial process and makes protective findings close to automatic for well-organized petitioners [S3].

The steel import certificate program imposes new paperwork and fees on every shipment, which small importers bear disproportionately, and gives domestic producers detailed competitor data they could use to coordinate market strategies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in import-battered industries like steel, the bill offered a real shot at relief, and by 2001 the domestic steel industry was in genuine distress. But the mechanism is one-directional: every easing of the injury test transfers money from the many (buyers of steel and protected goods) to the few (protected producers), and the bill's drafting — directing the commission how to weigh evidence, not just changing thresholds — would have made protection findings routine. The diffuse costs to steel-using industries and consumers plausibly exceeded the concentrated gains, which is the classic trade-off this kind of bill never states on its face.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on May 26, 2001, joined by original cosponsors including Rockefeller, Byrd, Hollings, Specter, and Mikulski [S1][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action afterward [S5].
The bill's cosponsor list totaled seven senators — six Democrats and one Republican — and no version ever advanced past referral [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-using manufacturers, importers, foreign steel exporters, and consumers were better off, because they avoided the higher prices and new permit costs the bill would have imposed. The domestic steel industry gained nothing from this vehicle, though the underlying push for import relief continued through other channels.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (six Democrats and one Republican), but no vote was ever held and no opposition was recorded, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill stacks every amendment in steel's favor: an easier safeguard test, looser antidumping factors, a permit-and-monitoring program tracking every steel shipment weekly, and rules for applying bilateral steel quotas. Its gains come from tariffs and quotas that raise steel prices for everyone else.

Easier tariffs and quotas on steel would raise their input costs, and they employ far more people than steelmaking does. Their interest in cheap imported steel runs alongside consumers' interest in lower prices.

industries.industry: Importers, customs brokers, and retailers of steel goods
industries.note: A new pre-entry certificate requirement, with fees and 30-day validity, adds cost and delay to every steel import; the bill also applies its remedies to Canadian and Mexican goods.

industries.industry: Perishable crop producers (fruit and vegetable growers)
industries.note: Season-by-season injury standards and the ability to count unpicked crops would make antidumping cases easier for seasonal growers, with costs passed to consumers in the form of fewer, pricier imports of produce.

industries.industry: Foreign steel exporters, including in Canada and Mexico
industries.note: The bill explicitly applies its remedies to goods from Canada and Mexico and eases treatment under bilateral quota arrangements, restricting their access to the US market.
